blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the policies that promote growth, trace how each works, and weigh how effective each is likely to be.

blocks.heading: The policy set
blocks.text: The policies that promote growth are macroeconomic policies: they act on the whole economy, not on one market or firm. On the demand side sit the fiscal measures of topic 4.3 - government spending and taxation - and the interest rate of topic 4.4. On the capacity side sit supply-side measures: education and training, infrastructure such as roads and ports, and incentives such as lower direct taxes. The Netherlands shows the capacity route outside southern Africa, with decades spent on flood defences that raised what its economy could produce.

blocks.heading: Demand-side, traced
blocks.text: Where the economy has spare capacity, a demand-side policy can raise output quickly. Trace a cut in the interest rate: borrowing becomes cheaper, so households bring forward purchases and firms fund investment; total spending rises, and firms meet it by hiring idle workers, so real GDP climbs as the economy moves toward its production possibility curve. At the curve already, the same policy finds no idle resources, and the extra spending tends to raise prices instead.

blocks.heading: Supply-side, traced
blocks.text: Capacity measures work more slowly and last longer. Trace a training programme: workers who produce more per hour let firms fill larger orders without larger workforces, so the economy's maximum output rises and the curve shifts outward. A new road to a port does the same: transport costs fall, exports reach distant markets at competitive prices, and firms expand production to meet the sales.

blocks.heading: Which policy, when
blocks.text: Effectiveness depends on where the economy stands. With idle resources, demand-side measures can lift output within a year or two; producing at the boundary, they mostly lift prices, and growth needs capacity measures instead. Capacity measures take years to arrive and need sustained finance, which a government with a thin tax base may struggle to hold. The choice turns on the economy's position, the time horizon it faces and the quality of its delivery.

blocks.heading: Macroeconomic is not microeconomic
blocks.text: The confusion: learners list measures acting on one market or firm as though they acted on the whole economy. The boundary: a macroeconomic policy works on economy-wide totals, while a microeconomic policy works on a single market or industry, such as a subsidy to one bus company. The test: ask what the measure reaches - the whole economy, or one part of it.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The fiscal and monetary tools named here are taught in topics 4.3 and 4.4, the supply-side measures in 4.5, and the aims they serve in 4.2.
